## Going right: delegated readers checked the session's claims against the works they rested on, and caught three of the assistant's errors before they merged

*2026-11-21 00:31:48 · retro*

<!-- inactive-ok-file: ADR-108 ADR-114 — Proposed; cited as open -->

**Reading after filing, with recollections marked, worked (pull requests
558 to 563).** Over 2026-11-20 and 21 the assistant filed claims relating
the record's rate and contraction results to μP, depth scaling, modular
duality and transformer interpretability, several of them resting on works
it knew only from memory. Each such work was registered Deferred, each
recollection was marked in the claim's text, and each claim's defeater
named the reading that would test it. The owner then asked to read
everything identified as due.

Sixteen readers ran in parallel, one per work, each with the full
read-and-file brief and its own notes branch ([ADR-108](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-108.md)). Fourteen read the
full text within about four minutes; two works were behind bot checks and
were read through neighbours ([ADR-114](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-114.md)). The filer rechecked every quotation
by script against the downloaded texts. All were found, though some only
after allowing for the PDF extraction's interleaved columns, which is worth
knowing: a naive string match reports false misses.

What made it work, worth keeping:

- **The brief asked for a recheck of the record after reading.** Readers
  found held entries the assistant had missed or denied: Freidlin and
  Wentzell and Berglund (the assistant had written that the record held
  neither), Dominé and colleagues on lazy and rich regimes, Geva and
  colleagues on depth.
- **Readers were asked for a verdict on the record's characterization.**
  Three corrections came back: semicontraction keeps nothing by itself (a
  claim had cited it as the general form of keeping a conserved part); the
  bounded hyperbolicity of a log commute-time geometry is trivial for any
  chain (a claim had stated it as content); middle transformer layers
  cannot be repeated (a claim had said they could).
- **Recollections were confirmed as often as corrected.** Depth-μP's
  learned change of order 1/L per block, and the modular norm's per-module
  mass, held. Marking them as recollections cost nothing and let the
  reading confirm or correct them directly.

To revisit: whether the file-then-read order should be the default for
claims that lean on unread works, or whether reading first would have
saved the revisions.

## Going right: the record already held most of the formal pieces, and the owner's reframings turned the assistant's first answers into better claims

*2026-11-21 00:31:49 · retro*

<!-- inactive-ok-file: CLAIM-635 THEORY-186 THEORY-2041 CLAIM-478 — Proposed; cited as open -->

**The record worked as memory.** In the session of 2026-11-20 the owner
asked a run of questions: how narrowing degrees of freedom relates to an
entry's life cycle, then to contraction, then to drift, hierarchy and
hyperbolicity, depth scaling. Each time, searching the record before
answering found that it already held a key formal piece: [CLAIM-635](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-635.md) (an
exactly conserved observable keeps information about the start), [THEORY-960](../../record/theory.d/THEORY-960.md)
(DeGroot's consensus keeps exactly πF), [CLAIM-581](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-581.md) (peak-cost thresholds are
an ultrametric), Saxe's deep linear dynamics ([THEORY-186](../../record/theory.d/THEORY-186.md), [THEORY-740](../../record/theory.d/THEORY-740.md)),
Schoenholz's depth scales ([THEORY-2041](../../record/theory.d/THEORY-2041.md)). The new results were mostly joins
between held entries, which is what the record is for.

**The owner's challenges improved the claims.** Twice the owner questioned
the framing of an answer, and both times the challenge was right:

- "Are you sure these are different things? … Isn't stabilization just
  monotone contraction?" The assistant had said forgetting a source and
  anchoring to it are different mechanisms. They are one contraction told
  apart by what each step conserves; the claim was rewritten before
  merging.
- "maybe I'm being brash calling it 'scale separation' and a more
  appropriate -- or at least easier to demonstrate -- assertion would call
  it 'rate differences'". Checking the sentence that prompted this found it
  wrong, and the restated claim (rate differences between levels exceeding
  those within) is both better supported and more precise. [CLAIM-478](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-478.md) took a
  new version.

**Checking by simulation before asserting** caught one error in time: a
designed hierarchy with noisy rates looked like it produced "a finer tree";
a direct comparison of tree topologies showed it kept the designed one, and
the claim was corrected before the owner built on it.

To revisit: the pattern of asking the assistant to relate a new idea to
the record's existing account, then challenging the framing, then filing.
It produced six pull requests in a day; whether that pace is sustainable
for review is a question for the retrospective.

## Going right: the owner noticed that a list in a decision should be a named class, so the decision extends without amendment

*2026-11-21 03:49:12 · retro · earmarked*

<!-- inactive-ok-file: ADR-127 — Proposed; the decision the note concerns -->

Earmarked for the retro by the owner, on pull request 570, 2026-11-21. The
draft of the dialectic regime ([ADR-127](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-127.md)) listed what it files without
asking as "claims, questions, terms, arguments, cases and leads". The owner:
"this class of items should probably have a referent so we can extend it
later and implicitly be included in the ADR. PS: this feels like a good
example of noticing a distinction."

**What went right.** A list in a rule is a closed set; a named class is
open. The list would have left a scheme added later outside the regime until
someone noticed and amended the decision. The revision names the class, the
argument schemes of [ADR-032](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-032.md) and those that have joined them, so it extends
as the record does.

**Why it may generalize.** It is the same move as the descriptor and
imposition distinction filed the same night: a rule stated by enumeration
describes the present set, while a rule stated by its referent holds as the
set grows. Worth a look, at the retro, at other decisions that enumerate
schemes or fields where they mean a class.

**What is still missing.** The referent is prose. `luria.yaml` has no field
marking a scheme as part of the record's own argument, so nothing checks
membership. A field would be the next rung, and a change to `luria.yaml`, so
the owner's to make.

## Going wrong, twice: a code in a title fails docs-check, because repair links the code in the heading and not in the title

*2026-11-21 04:22:08 · retro*

<!-- inactive-ok-file: POSTMORTEM-004 — the review of the first time -->

**What happened.** On 2026-11-21 docs-check failed on pull request 571 with
one violation: [ADR-122](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-122.md)'s `title:` and its body heading disagreed. The
title said "as [ADR-068](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-068.md) does for filing"; the repair had linked the code in
the heading, `[ADR-068](ADR-068.md)`, and left the title bare, so the lint's
title-matches-heading check failed. The fix was to take the code out of the
title. This is the failure [POSTMORTEM-004](../../record/postmortems.d/POSTMORTEM-004.md) reviewed the same night, for a
code in [ARG-124](../../record/arguments.d/ARG-124.md)'s title (now [ARG-124](../../record/arguments.d/ARG-124.md)), which also failed docs-check.

**Why it recurred.** The postmortem recorded the rule, no code in a title,
as something to remember. The assistant wrote three alternative decisions
in one script, and the rule was not in the script. A rule kept in memory
fails the second time a filer is busy.

**What to change.** Luria's own principle applies: a guard that keeps
catching you is a bug report about the workflow. Two upstream fixes, either
of which removes the hazard: the repair could leave a heading's codes as it
leaves the title's, or the title check could compare the two with links
stripped. Short of that, `luria new` could refuse a title containing a code.
Not filed upstream yet; for the owner's call, and for the retro.

## Going wrong: the owner ruled by ticking a checklist, and the assistant read only the comment

*2026-11-21 06:53:44 · retro*

<!-- inactive-ok-file: ADR-124 — Proposed; the decision whose first pass this concerns -->

On pull request 579 the adoption review put its verdicts to the owner as a
checklist. The owner ticked the two adopt groups and left a comment ruling
the third. The comment arrived as an event; the ticks did not, since editing
a description sends none. The assistant applied the comment, reported the
two adopt groups as undecided and asked again. The owner: "sorry for the
confusion, my checking the boxes you provided was intended as a go-ahead
signal".

**Why.** The assistant offered a checklist and then read only the channel
that notifies it. A ruling can arrive by a channel that does not notify.

**What changed.** [ADR-124](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-124.md) and the adoption-review skill now say a ticked
box is a ruling, and the pass reads the description's checklist as well as
the comments before applying anything. The same holds for any pull request
that offers the owner a checklist, such as the status review's under
[ADR-057](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-057.md).

## Going wrong, caught: resolving a merge conflict with --ours reverted three of the owner's rulings

*2026-11-21 07:01:19 · retro*

Merging staging into pull request 579 conflicted on three alternative
decisions, [ADR-118](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-118.md), [ADR-122](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-122.md) and [ADR-123](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-123.md). The conflicting
hunks were only the directive lines CI's repair rewrites, so the assistant
resolved them with `git checkout --ours`. That takes the whole file, not
the hunk: the branch was cut before the owner's rulings in pull request 578,
so the three went back from Rejected to Proposed. The assistant saw it on
checking the result, restored staging's versions before anything merged,
and confirmed the other files from 577 and 578 were untouched.

**What to change.** Resolve a conflict hunk by hunk, never with
`--ours` or `--theirs` on a file that the other side changed beyond the
conflict; and after any merge resolution, diff the touched files against
the side that was not kept.

## Going wrong, a fourth time: a code in a title failed docs-check, after a retrospective written the same hour named the hazard

*2026-11-21 09:05:39 · retro*

**What happened.** On pull request 594 docs-check failed on three alternative decisions. Each title began "Alternative A to [ADR-075](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-075.md)'s step 5". The repair linked the code in each body heading and not in the title, so the lint's title-matches-heading check failed. The fix was to take the code out of the titles ("Alternative A for the admission test of a synthesis").

**Why it recurred.** This is the fourth occurrence: [ARG-124](../../record/arguments.d/ARG-124.md)'s title ([POSTMORTEM-004](../../record/postmortems.d/POSTMORTEM-004.md)), [ADR-122](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-122.md)'s (the devlog entry of 04:22:08), an account's on pull request 557, and now these three. [RETRO-006](../../record/retrospectives.d/RETRO-006.md), filed the same hour by the same assistant, named the third. Upstream luria refuses codes in titles (dmarx/luria#403). This record's docs workflow pins luria 1.10.0, which does not; 1.11.0 is released, and its `luria new` refuses such a title with a message saying why (checked on 2026-11-21 in a scratch environment). A rule kept in memory failed again, while the filer was writing ten pull requests in a row.

**What to change.** Bump the pinned luria to 1.11.0, in `.github/workflows/docs.yml` and wherever sessions install it, so that `luria new` refuses a code in a title at the moment it is written. Until then, a filer writing a title that names a decision or a claim should write the thing, not the code ("the admission test of a synthesis", not "[ADR-075](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-075.md)'s step 5"). The bump is a tooling change, for the owner.

## Going wrong, caught before merge: a hand-rolled script to rewrite temporary codes after the promotion also rewrote the formerly: fields, and was not needed, since luria repair already makes that rewrite

*2026-11-21 09:37:39 · retro*

**What happened.** After the owner merged the promotion pull request (582) into main, its codes were made permanent, and four open pull requests still cited the old temporary codes. The assistant merged staging into each and ran a script that replaced every temporary code with its permanent one, using each entry's `formerly:` field as the map. The script also replaced the codes inside `formerly:` itself, so [CLAIM-181](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-181.md)'s history read `formerly: CLAIM-181`. That happened in 24 entries on one branch and a few on others. Three of the branches were pushed before the assistant noticed that the rewrite had touched many more files than it expected.

**How it was found.** Before pushing the fourth branch, the assistant read one rewritten file instead of trusting the count.

**The fix.** `git revert` of the three pushed commits, and a rewrite that skips the `formerly:` list. A check over every file each branch changes then found no stale temporary code left. No branch's history was rewritten, and nothing reached staging.

**What to keep.** The script was not needed at all. The owner asked whether luria already does this, and it does. `luria repair`, which the pull request's docs-check runs, upgrades a concretized code's old spelling wherever it appears, through `doc_refs.upgrade_legacy_spellings`, and skips `formerly:`. It does so in the pinned 1.10.0 as well as in 1.11.0. Nothing was needed after the promotion at all. Until a branch is merged, its own copy of each cited entry still carries the temporary code, so the code resolves there. After it merges, an old spelling resolves through `formerly:` with a `legacy-spellings` warning, not a lint failure. It is rewritten at the next repair, by the branch's docs-check on its next push or by docs-generate on main at the next promotion. The back-merge needs no repair step: main has just been repaired, and staging's own changes were repaired on their pull requests (the owner asked; the answer was to leave it as it is). A hand-rolled rewrite duplicated a mechanical repair CI already makes, against [ADR-054](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-054.md), and got it wrong. Before writing a script for a mechanical change to the record, check `luria --help` and `luria repair`'s list of repairs.

## Going wrong, caught by the owner: asked the owner which of three senses of separability was meant instead of filing all three, against the dialectic regime's rule on readings

*2026-11-21 18:29:55 · retro*

**What happened.** The owner asked whether the record had an account of "the notion of separability raised in the conversation" (the exchange "Rich Get Richer Power Laws"). The assistant found three senses in the exchange: separation of scales or levels, separation of classes, and spectral separation. It mapped each to held entries and proposed a term and a note. Then it asked: "Which sense did you mean? If it was sense 1 in the critical case, the note on [SYNTHESIS-054](../../record/syntheses.d/SYNTHESIS-054.md) is the substantive part." The owner's go-ahead ("dialectic on") adopted that lean. So the term, which covers all three, was filed, but the substantive note was filed for sense 1 only.

**How it was found.** The owner: "one of the conventions of the dialectic regime is supposed to be that when you encounter ambiguity in how a phrase might be interpreted, you file all of the available options (within reason). err on the side of adding richness to the record." CLAUDE.md says so: "When a turn admits several valid readings that would be filed differently, file each, marked as alternatives, and say which is which; the owner chooses."

**The fix.** Notes for senses 2 and 3 as well: on [SYNTHESIS-109](../../record/syntheses.d/SYNTHESIS-109.md) (what can be told apart, with the spectral threshold as a budgeted telling-apart) and on [SYNTHESIS-083](../../record/syntheses.d/SYNTHESIS-083.md) (a readout separates what the spectrum does not show). The term was also added to the two accounts of the exchange.

**What to keep.** The rule was applied in the same session's filing, where U5 and U23 each got two readings filed as alternatives. It was not applied to a question about the record, as if a question were not a turn. The question was a turn, and its ambiguity changed what would be filed. A question that ends "which did you mean?" while the regime is on is the sign. File each reading, then say which the assistant leans to. Note too how the go-ahead worked: because it adopts a stated lean ([ADR-127](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-127.md)), a lean stated in place of filing the alternatives narrows the filing to that lean.

## Going wrong, caught by the owner: Rejected arguments titled with their conclusions, so that rejecting a route read as rejecting a conclusion the owner thinks probably true

*2026-11-21 21:27:15 · retro*

**What happened.** The filing of "Rich Get Richer Power Laws" made five Rejected ARGs. The assistant wrote their titles as the inferences' conclusions, for example "The behaviour of sloppy models carries over to overparameterized neural networks…". Each body said that only the route failed. But the title is what the index shows, and with "Rejected" beside it the title read as the conclusion refuted.

**How it was found.** The owner, asking about the choice of keeping them Rejected or filing each failure as a claim: "populating the arg with the prose of the conclusion and marking it rejected predisposes future inquiry to treat that conclusion (which I think is actually probably correct) as rejected, rather than this particular path to that conclusion as rejected. maybe we need to be more careful about how we construct our args?"

**The fix.** Two alternative decisions, [ADR-136](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-136.md) (route first; a standing sentence) and [ADR-138](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-138.md) (title as verdict), with the five ARGs retitled under the first. The owner's view that the conclusion probably holds is now its own claim, [CLAIM-801](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-801.md).

**What to keep.** The assistant's own previous answer framed the choice as "keep Rejected, or file the failure as a claim". That framing missed the point, because it treated the failure as the thing worth stating, when the conclusion was the thing at risk. A title has to survive being read without its status's meaning in mind. Of the record's 40 Rejected ARGs, most lead with their grounds ("X shows that Y"), which mostly survives that reading. The ones that state the bare conclusion are what the sweep under [ADR-136](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-136.md) would fix.

## Going wrong, caught by CI: merging a pull request into staging while a promotion's docs-generate was running made the back-merge conflict on the two files both had changed

*2026-11-21 22:58:34 · retro*

**What happened.** The owner merged the promotion pull request (610) into main at about 22:44. Its docs-generate made the batch's temporary codes permanent: [ADR-137](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-137.md) became [ADR-137](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-137.md) and [RETRO-008](../../record/retrospectives.d/RETRO-008.md) became [RETRO-008](../../record/retrospectives.d/RETRO-008.md). While that was running, the assistant merged pull request 614 into staging. 614 set [ADR-137](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-137.md) Active and [RETRO-008](../../record/retrospectives.d/RETRO-008.md) Accepted. When docs-generate finished, the back-merge of main into staging found the same two files changed on both sides and stopped: "main does not merge cleanly into staging; resolve by hand".

**How it was found.** The Docs workflow on main failed in its back-merge job. The assistant was waiting for the back-merge before filing the next batch, and saw the failure when it checked.

**The fix.** A branch cut from staging, with `origin/main` merged into it. Each conflict was resolved by keeping main's concretized file (its number, `formerly:` and permanent codes) and reapplying 614's edits by script: status, version 2 and history, `prompted`, and the responses section. The branch then went to staging as a pull request. The old spellings left in 614's own new files are upgraded by `luria repair` in the pull request's docs-check, so they were not rewritten by hand.

**What to keep.** Between a merge into main and its back-merge, staging should take no merges that edit entries in the batch being promoted. The promotion is concretizing those very files. The next merge into staging waits for the back-merge commit, or for the back-merge job's failure, as here.

## Going wrong, caught by the owner: read the owner's bulk as the many directions when the owner meant the dominant ones, and treated a falling training loss as less than learning

*2026-11-22 00:44:15 · retro*

**What happened.** Relaying the reading of Song, Ahn and Yun, the assistant wrote that their "bulk" means "everything outside the top k, not the small-eigenvalue tail", and that the paper "doesn't show that small directions carry information", because "'Learning' here means only that the training loss falls". The filed notes on [QUESTION-511](../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-511.md) and [NOTE-2250](../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2250.md) repeated the second point.

**How it was found.** The owner: "you have my intended meaning of 'bulk' backwards, I meant that in the sense of the domain which carries the dominant density. in the context of e.g. the 80-20 rule, the *bulk* of the population does not contribute the *bulk* of the activity. Spectrally, the top eigenvalues definitionally are associated with the dominating 'bulk' of the operator's activity." And: "training loss falling is evidence that learning is happening. the capabilities are being measurably developed. "learning" doesn't just mean the loss is falling, that's a measure of the learning that is happening, which is concretely the changes that are happening within the organization of the model's representational space."

**The fix.** [TERM-143](../../record/terms.d/TERM-143.md) separates the bulk by count from the bulk by weight. Dated corrections on [QUESTION-511](../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-511.md) and [NOTE-2250](../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2250.md) say what Song et al. do show in the owner's terms: capability develops through the non-dominant directions.

**What to keep.** Two habits gave the slip. The first took a source's technical word, Song's "bulk subspace", for the owner's ordinary one. The second set the bar for "learning" at decodability, so that the paper's own measure of learning counted for less. When a source and the owner use the same word, say which sense is meant before arguing from it.

## Going right: relaying each reading as it returned caught overreaching support judgements before they were filed; going wrong: a usage limit stopped all three filers at once, and the branch took work-in-progress commits

*2026-11-22 04:15:00 · retro*

<!-- inactive-ok-file: ARG-141 CLAIM-795 CLAIM-841 — Proposed, Rejected, Deferred or new; the entries this filing made or touched -->

**Going right.** Following [ADR-140](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-140.md), each reader's report was relayed to the owner as it came in, with what it changed. Doing that in the chat, before any filing, put the overreaches in plain view while they were cheap to fix: [CLAIM-841](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-841.md) grounded on a paper that never mentions criticality, [ARG-141](../../record/arguments.d/ARG-141.md) resting tests on a paper that has none, [CLAIM-795](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-795.md) citing Newman for all seven mechanisms when he covers four, and [LIT-2983](../../record/literature.d/LIT-2983.md)'s summary placing the spike in the features rather than the weights. Each went to the filers as a named correction, and two became Rejected ARGs whose summaries keep the conclusion's standing apart from the route ([ADR-136](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-136.md)). Asking the readers to recheck the record after reading also found held entries the first search missed, around ten per work.

**Going wrong.** All three filers ran in parallel and hit the account's usage limit together, minutes in. They were resumed from their transcripts and finished, but the stop hook asked for commits while they were still editing, so the branch carries work-in-progress commits that cut across filers. That is not what [ADR-139](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-139.md)'s rule meant, which was to commit each worker's listed files when it finishes. The pull request was held back until all three were done, so that CI's repair would not land on the branch mid-edit.

**What to keep.** Keep relaying before filing; it is where the corrections came from. When parallel workers may be cut off, commit in progress under a plain "work in progress" message, and open the pull request only once the workers have finished.

## Going right: a claim of the record's own was run against the defeater it stated in advance, and failed it; the admission written a day earlier had named the route and the sentence that would survive it

*2026-11-22 07:35:00 · retro*

<!-- inactive-ok-file: CLAIM-778 CASE-307 CLAIM-864 CLAIM-863 — Proposed or Open; the claim, its lead, the study and its two readings -->

**What happened.** [CLAIM-778](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-778.md) (filed 2026-11-20) stated its defeater as a count the record could run on itself: cited claims revised no less often, at matched age, than uncited ones. [LEAD-199](../../record/leads.d/LEAD-199.md) specified the count the same day. Run on 2026-11-22 ([CASE-307](../../record/cases.d/CASE-307.md)), it met the defeater: cited claims are revised about 1.45 times as often.

**Why it went right.** Three things made the result usable rather than arguable. The defeater was written before the data, in terms a script could check. [LEAD-199](../../record/leads.d/LEAD-199.md) fixed the design (population, what counts as substantive, exposure, age matching) before anyone looked, so the analyst's choices were few and stated. And the synthesis review's admission of 2026-11-21 had already named the confound that would produce this result (scrutiny follows citation) and the narrower sentence that would survive it, so the two readings ([CLAIM-864](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-864.md), [CLAIM-863](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-863.md)) were filed from text the record already held, not improvised after the fact.

**What to keep.** State defeaters as checks the record can run on itself, and specify the lead's design when the claim is filed. Keep admissions that say in advance how a claim could fail: they turn a refutation into a choice between readings instead of a dispute.

## Going wrong: work held until the end was lost or put at risk three ways in one day, though the morning's note had already drawn the lesson

*2026-11-22 10:40:30 · retro*

<!-- inactive-ok-file: ADR-108 ADR-141 ADR-142 — Proposed or new; the reader rule, and the two alternative decisions this note led to -->

**Going wrong.** The owner, at 10:36: "this keeps happening repeatedly. it is an expensive mistake and I'd like it if we didn't keep making it." Three things went wrong.

- **The sweep lost its results.** The assistant's own background sweep of the 184 Unfetched works wrote its results file only at the end. It ran under the default background time limit of 30 minutes, and was stopped at 162. Its pace (18 works in 12 minutes) had said two hours. The assistant read the pace, noted "about two hours", and changed nothing.
- **The lead workers were briefed to commit at the end.** Their brief, kept in the scratchpad, read "if you hit an API usage limit, commit and push what you have". A hard stop leaves no turn for that.
- **The briefs and the triage were scratchpad files**, so they would have gone with the container.

**Wrong theory, and how it was found out.** The theory was that [ADR-108](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-108.md) had dealt with this. It had dealt with it for readers only. The loss showed where the rule stopped: everything that was not a reader. The 04:15 note had said, "When parallel workers may be cut off, commit in progress." Nobody put that into a brief, so the same lesson was drawn twice in six hours.

**What to change.** Two alternative decisions are filed: [ADR-141](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-141.md), which supersedes [ADR-108](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-108.md) with one general rule, and [ADR-142](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-142.md), which adds a sibling to it. Both carry the same first application. The lead-worker brief now lives in the repository as the run-lead skill, with pushes after every step, a PROGRESS file, per-item results and a time budget. The running sweep is checkpointed into its branch every ten minutes, and the three workers then running were told to push at once. A lesson in a devlog note should become a step in a brief the same day, or it will be learned again.

## A dynamics reading lead: per-work commits held a fifteen-work reading batch together, and one careless shell command broke /dev/null for every worker on the machine

*2026-11-22 15:59:10 · retro*

**Going right.** The run-lead skill's rule of one commit and push per step
held up across a fifteen-work batch: each work's NOTE, THEORY, LIT version
and dated notes went in one commit, with PROGRESS.md updated in the same
push, so a stop at any point would have lost one work at most. Small
helper scripts kept in the scratchpad (one moving a LIT to its new version
from a JSON spec, one appending a dated note, one checking every double
quotation against the downloaded text, one listing cited codes not in
force and not excused) made the fourteen filings uniform and let every
quotation be checked by script rather than by eye. Reading in the order of
what the claims most needed put the works with concrete bearings
([QUESTION-063](../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-063.md), [CLAIM-153](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-153.md), [QUESTION-252](../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-252.md)) first, which is where the one new
claim came from.

**Going wrong.** To discard a scaffolded NOTE the worker ran
`mv <file> /dev/null` as root. That replaced the device with a regular
file, which other workers on the same machine would then have written
into and read from. It was noticed on the next command and the device
recreated (`mknod -m 666 /dev/null c 1 3`) within a minute; nothing else
was seen to fail. The safe idiom is `rm` on the file, or `git clean` on a
path the worker created. A shared machine turns a private slip into
everyone's.

**Also.** The worktree guard refused several compound commands (heredocs
mixed with `git`, or text the guard could not parse). Writing inputs to
files with the editor and running one plain command per call always
passed; batching edits and commits into one shell line did not.

## Filing a seventeen-turn exchange: five section workers in one tree, with the thesis that runs across their sections kept for the lead

*2026-11-22 22:55:20 · retro*

**Going right, so far.** The exchange "Explain First Contact RL" runs to
seventeen owner turns and about 240 KB of visible text, and ChatGPT read the
record from main before answering: every one of the 71 codes it cited
exists, and their titles match what it cited them for. So the filing is
mostly a map, and the work is in the parts the record does not hold.

The lead read the whole transcript first, then split it by stretch of turns
into five section workers (First Contact and the scroll interface;
dispositions and the self; Luria, flow, team and singularity; ecology,
measures and the representation hypotheses; regulation), forks that share
the lead's reading. Each got the codes its stretch cites, the ledger items
the lead had listed, and the rule from [ADR-139](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-139.md): list every file, append
dated notes at the end of a held file and retry on a failed edit, commit
nothing. Temporary codes are random, so parallel `luria new` calls cannot
collide.

**A choice worth checking at the retro.** One thesis, about what a self is,
recurs across four of the five stretches (A13, A15, A21 to A22, A24, A26,
A29), each version revising the last. Giving it to any one worker would
have made that worker wait on the codes the others file. Instead each
worker files its own versions as ChatGPT's claims, and the lead audits the
whole lineage under step 9b once all five have reported. Whether that left
the lineage's account thinner than a single owner would have made it is the
question for the retrospective.

**Going wrong, and caught by CI.** Twenty-two of the entries the section
workers drafted had a body heading shorter than the title, or a heading
missing its code prefix. Each worker had run the narrow reference scan,
which does not check headings, and so each reported its files clean.
docs-check failed the pull request with one violation per file. The fix
was mechanical: each heading rewritten from the title, then checked with
`luria.lint.check_title`, the check docs-check itself runs. The step was
missing from the read-and-file skill, which now states it. A brief for
drafters should carry it too.

**A scaffold bug.** `luria new curation --title "..."` (luria 1.11.0)
wrote a title containing "owner's" as a single-quoted YAML string with
the apostrophe escaped as `\'`. YAML needs `''` there. docs-check's
repair step then failed to parse the journal entry. The other scaffolds
in this filing (claims, terms, the synthesis) quoted correctly, or had no
apostrophe. Fixed by hand. Every changed file's front matter was then
parsed with PyYAML before pushing. Worth an issue on luria, left for the
owner.

## A code-rewriting merge step overwrote the temporary codes in formerly lists, on fifty-six entries

*2026-11-23 00:53:40 · retro*

**Going wrong, found by the owner.** The owner noticed that temporary codes
had gone from `formerly:` lists. They had not been deleted: each list held
the entry's own concrete code in their place, so [CLAIM-626](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-626.md) listed itself
as formerly [CLAIM-626](../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-626.md).

The cause was a back-merge of staging into a lead's branch after a
promotion (commit b23754a0, merged with pull request 746). Its message
says the conflict hunks kept the branch's side "with every temporary code
that a staging entry lists under formerly: written as that entry's
code". That rewrite was meant for citations. Applied to every
occurrence, it also hit the `formerly:` field, where the temporary code
is the point. Both parents of that merge held the right list, and the
merge result did not. That cost 28 entries on staging.

**The wrong theory, and how it fell.** The first search looked for
removed `formerly` lines and found only link repairs. A comparison of
`formerly` lists between main and staging found the 28. The first guess
was a conflict resolved to the branch's stale copy. Reading the two
parents showed both had the list right, so the merge had rewritten it.
A scan for any entry whose `formerly` contains its own code then found
28 more, already on main from earlier merges, which predate this
session's clone depth. A deeper fetch of main's history recovered them
from each entry's first concretized version.

**The fix.** All 56 were restored. A check now passes: no entry lists
itself, every front matter parses, and no temporary code is claimed by
two entries. The run-lead skill states the rule. At the owner's word ("may as
well add that check upstream on luria"), the lint check is proposed
upstream in dmarx/luria pull request 404: an entry whose `formerly`
contains its own code fails the lint ([DP-3](../design-principles.md#dp-3)). Fired on this record's
staging before the repair, it found the same 56 entries. It found none
after.

## Resumable study scripts that were resumable only when nothing went wrong

*2026-11-23 01:05:31 · retro*

**Going wrong, found by review.** [LEAD-175](../../record/leads.d/LEAD-175.md)'s scripts were written
resumable, and the run-lead skill asks for that: computations persist per
item. But the persistence was two writes where it needed one, or a
completion key coarser than what was written. In `posterior.py` the
output and the sampler state were saved separately. In `sgd_sweep.py` one
written line marked a whole job done. Both are safe when a run either
finishes or never starts, and unsafe exactly in the case resumability
exists for. Nothing caught it, because no test interrupted a write. A code
review the owner forwarded found both.

**What fixed it, and the lesson.**
- Write the progress marker and the state as one atomic unit. Here that is
  a checkpoint replaced by rename after the output line is synced.
- Reconcile on start, and stop when reconciliation fails.
- Key completion on exactly what each line records.
- Test the interruption itself, in `test_resume.py`.

The run-lead skill's persistence step could say so. That is left as a
proposal: a change to the skill's step is a procedure change, and only one
lead has shown the need.

**Audit.** The committed SGD results are complete. The posterior outputs
are consistent, but cannot show that no stale resume happened, so that
part is stated as likely, not shown. The note on [LEAD-175](../../record/leads.d/LEAD-175.md) says which.

**Going wrong, found by the owner.** Asked to "file it as a work" for the
manuscript ChatGPT drafted at U24 and U25 of "Explain First Contact RL",
the assistant read "work" as the LIT scheme's sense, a work read from
outside, and filed a LIT. The owner meant the `works` vocabulary, a
manuscript the record's claims are marshalled into, which [ADR-104](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-104.md) and
[ADR-106](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-106.md) had used twice before for manuscripts drafted the same way. The

labels the LIT scheme "Works", and the `works` field is "a manuscript the
record's claims are marshalled into". The read-and-file skill speaks only
of the first. The signal that should have decided it was the source: an
assistant's draft written at the owner's request from the record's own
entries is the record's argument, not a reading, and both precedents said
so.

an exchange to be filed, check the `works` vocabulary and [ADR-104](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-104.md) first.

<a id="20261123034500"></a>

## The write-manuscript protocol was first written from one manuscript's README, not from the record of how that manuscript was made

*2026-11-23 03:45:00 · retro*

**Going wrong, found by the owner.** Asked to document a procedure for
fleshing out a manuscript from the record, the assistant wrote
[ADR-143](../../record/decisions.d/ADR-143.md) and the write-manuscript skill from the first manuscript's
README, its review file and its directory layout. The owner asked whether
it took into account the procedure actually used: the notes about that
process, the retrospectives and curation entries on it, and its commit and
pull request messages. It did not. The README is that draft's own summary,
written by the same hands, and says what was done, not what went wrong or
what the reviews of it recommended.

**Why it happened.** The README looked like a complete account of the
procedure, so it was taken as the source rather than as one source. A
procedure is what practice converged on, and the record keeps that
convergence in its journals (curation, devlog, retrospectives) and in git,
not in the artifact.

**What was done.** A reader was sent to mine those records and compare them
with the skill; the skill and the ADR are revised on its report in the same
pull request, before the new manuscript's review.

**What would catch it.** When writing down a procedure from practice, read
the record of the practice (journals, retrospectives, commits, pull
requests) as well as its product.
